source_batch.unit_label: Module D unit 3 (courseware unit 28): compliance governance structure and internal controls

facts.statement: Organisational structure of compliance (courseware, pp. 593-594): Board of directors; Audit Committee of the Board (ACB); managing or executive director; an independent Compliance department headed by the Chief Compliance Officer; compliance function at the verticals in the corporate office; compliance function at field offices (Field General Managers' offices wherever they exist, regional offices, zonal offices, branches). The CCO has direct reporting lines to the MD and CEO and/or the Board or its Committee; if the CCO reports to the MD and CEO the ACB meets the CCO quarterly one-to-one without senior management. Business and functional departments should report directly to the CCO on compliance, and Compliance Officers at regional and zonal offices report to the CCO directly. The CCO reviews the performance of all Compliance Officers in the bank, and the Board or ACB reviews the CCO's performance appraisal.
facts.locator: S01 printed pp. 593-594; CCO line confirmed by RBI_CCO_2020 paragraph 2.7

facts.statement: Board responsibility for compliance (RBI circular of 11 September 2020): the Board of Directors is overall responsible for overseeing the effective management of the compliance function and compliance risk; the MD and CEO ensures an independent compliance function and adherence to the compliance policy; the Board-approved policy is reviewed at least once a year and includes a quality assurance and improvement programme that is independently externally reviewed at least once in three years; the compliance function is subject to internal audit.

Board duties as the courseware states them: ensure an appropriate compliance policy is in place and oversee its implementation; ensure compliance issues are resolved effectively and expeditiously by senior management with the help of the CCO and compliance staff; ensure there is no potential conflict of interest and that the compliance function's activities are independently reviewed at least once in three years, with the compliance and audit functions kept separate; review compliance functions quarterly and the status of implementation annually; delegate these tasks, if needed, to the ACB, which may also review the status of audit functions and performance, with the Board issuing directions on improvement. The Companies Act, 2013 casts a responsibility on directors to devise proper systems to ensure compliance with all applicable laws, confirmed in the Directors' Responsibility Statement in the directors' report to shareholders.

Senior management and the compliance function (RBI circular of 11 September 2020): the CCO is selected through a well-defined process on recommendation of a senior executive level selection committee constituted by the Board, which recommends candidates in order of merit and the Board takes the final decision; the Department of Supervision, RBI Central Office, receives prior intimation of appointment, premature transfer or removal, supported by a detailed profile, the fit and proper certification of the MD and CEO and the rationale for changes. The compliance function: apprises the Board and senior management of regulations, rules, standards and developments; clarifies compliance issues; assesses compliance risk at least once a year and develops a risk-oriented activity plan submitted to the ACB for approval and made available to internal audit; reports promptly to the Board, ACB or MD and CEO on major changes or observations; periodically reports compliance failures and breaches to the Board or ACB and circulates them to functional heads; monitors and periodically tests compliance with sufficient, representative compliance testing, placing results before the Board, ACB or MD and CEO; examines sustenance of compliance; and ensures supervisory observations of RBI and other directions are complied with in letter and spirit in a time bound and sustainable manner. The courseware adds the identification of the main compliance risks facing the bank at least once a year.
facts.locator: RBI_CCO_2020 paragraphs 2.5, 2.6 and 2.9; S01 printed pp. 595-596

facts.statement: Compliance department at the corporate office (courseware): a department of formal status at the central or head office, headed by a senior executive designated as CCO (preferably General Manager or equivalent, not below two levels from the CEO, who may be recruited from the market) with overall responsibility for coordinating the identification of compliance issues and managing compliance risk. The basis for identifying compliance requirements: RBI master circulars and directions consolidated and updated, RBI guidelines issued from time to time, laws and statutes applicable to banks, and the bank's internal guidelines and policies. The basis for assessing compliance risk: regulatory focus, nature of activity (whether inherently high risk), the bank's exposure to it (materiality) and breaches reported in the past (history). Compliance staff are never assigned audit or inspection duties because of conflict of interest; the compliance function is subject to independent review and compliance and audit are kept separate. The department frames a mechanism for coordination with functional departments, field offices and branches, and has adequate, well-qualified staff, preferably with knowledge of law, accountancy and information technology and practical experience in business lines and audit or inspection functions.

Functions of the compliance department (courseware): identify business functions under each statutory and regulatory guideline; assess compliance risk by business line, product and process and formulate mitigation proposals; ensure prompt dissemination of regulator and Ministry of Finance guidelines to head office functional departments, controlling and field offices and obtain conclusive compliance reported to the ACB quarterly; build communication systems between branches and zonal compliance departments and overseas centres; ensure functional departments have function-wise compliance parameters for their staff and list returns; circulate compliance failures and preventive instructions; sit on the Product Group Committee to vet new products and services from the compliance angle and monitor new products intensively for six months after introduction; coordinate closely with business operations and guide staff on interpretation; provide inspectors and concurrent auditors a compliance checklist and have audit findings scrutinised; conduct compliance testing on a sample basis in selected zones quarterly and report results to the MD and CEO; coordinate with RBI's Senior Supervisory Manager team in risk based supervision and submit data for Tranches I, IA, IB, II and III after review at DGM or AGM level; coordinate submission of returns and replies to RBI queries; guide operational departments on cross-border business compliance. The CCO is the nodal contact between the bank and RBI; directions from other regulators (IRDA, SEBI and so on) are handled by their separate compliance officers, and any discomfort conveyed by another regulator is brought to RBI's notice through the CCO.

Reporting by the compliance department (courseware): compliance rules submitted by branches and zones monthly or quarterly are consolidated for the ACB; the MIS includes a monthly report through executive directors or the CMD to the Board on important RBI and Ministry of Finance communications, a quarterly report to the ACB on the status of the compliance function, a summarised quarterly report to the ACB on RBI and MOF communications (functional departments give feedback on communications from self-regulatory bodies such as IBA, FEDAI and FIMMDA to the compliance department within seven days), a yearly report to the Board on the assessment of compliance risk, a report to the Board whenever material compliance failures occur (exception basis), and a report to the executive director or CMD on the results of random test checks. For overseas establishments the department ensures policies, specifically KYC-AML and compliance, are updated and reviewed not more than a year ago; obtains periodic confirmations including a monthly Compliance Sustainability Tracker, monthly certificates on regulatory violations and penalties, and quarterly reports on new regulations; ensures overseas compliance officers conduct independent compliance testing, currently quarterly; and reports status to the top management and ACB.

CCO and committees: the CCO is not a member of any committee that conflicts with the role, including any committee dealing with purchases or sanctions, and if a member has only an advisory role (RBI circular). The courseware adds that the CCO may be a member or invitee of the Audit Committee of the Board or Audit Committee of Executives, the Credit Risk Management Committee, the Committee for Operational Risk Management and the Product Group Committee, and the MD and CEO or executive directors may decide the CCO's participation in other committees.
facts.locator: RBI_CCO_2020 paragraph 2.12; S01 printed p. 599 for the list of committees

facts.statement: Functional departments at head office (courseware): they set up systems for meticulous compliance with statutory, regulatory and internal guidelines and promptly report any breach in their area to the compliance department, which scrutinises it and guides rectification. Each functional head designates a senior officer, at least in scale IV or V, as the department's compliance officer to identify and assess compliance risk in the functional area, prepare a mitigation plan with the compliance department and make time bound reports. That officer identifies compliance issues from guidelines and sends a consolidated list to the compliance department, acts on issues the department identifies, monitors compliance and reports at the stipulated frequency, maintains registers of returns and follows up with originating units, ensures timely submission of regulatory returns and that agendas and review notes go to the Board, ACB and the Supervisory Committee on Risk, shares experience, joins compliance training and converts guidelines into actionable instructions (technology flags, mandatory or exception reports, job cards, manuals, training). Functional departments build compliance culture, vet the quality and integrity of data and reports submitted to RBI before the top executives and the Chairman or ACB submit them, hold prime responsibility for monitoring compliance in their areas, update manuals and codes of conduct (which are available on the bank's website), forward RBI and MOF communications for action, and submit a compliance certificate to the head office compliance department at quarterly intervals; the compliance department places a quarterly note before the ACB confirming compliance with RBI and MOF circulars.

Field level structure (courseware): the branch is the front line unit in the compliance hierarchy; branch managers and staff play a crucial role because products are delivered and serviced there, and conflict of interest between managing compliance risk and business development cannot be fully avoided, so it must not be allowed to get in the way; the branch manager, accountant and officers are primarily responsible for compliance and the branch manager also functions as the branch's compliance officer. Compliance officers are designated in Field General Manager, zonal and regional offices; they report directly to the CCO and apprise the FGM, zonal manager or regional head of compliance levels and breaches. The compliance function at RO, ZO or FGMO reports to the central compliance department, submits quarterly status of its command area including branches and functional departments in a prescribed format, reports and escalates breaches observed (through audit or visit reports) immediately, and, through the Internal Control and Inspection department, covers compliance in routine inspections; the role of the zonal or regional office in branch compliance is handholding, trouble shooting and monitoring.

Overseas centres (courseware): each centre covering a cluster of foreign branches or representative offices has an independent compliance department headed by a local compliance officer, preferably or and an India based officer in Scale III or IV supported by local staff; the centre's compliance officer has a dotted line to the CCO, monitors the compliance functions of the branches in the centre, sends monthly reports and findings to the CCO, conducts compliance testing periodically (preferably quarterly) and submits it independently to the CCO. The chief executive of the centre implements the bank's compliance policy or territory-based local guidelines, whichever is more stringent. A dedicated overseas compliance desk at head office provides oversight and timely reporting to top management, the ACB, the Board and RBI.

Supporting functions (courseware): Human Resources provides the compliance department sufficient, appropriately skilled staff, preferably with knowledge of law, accountancy and IT and experience in business lines and audit or inspection. Learning and Development arranges regular training for compliance staff in new products, corporate governance, risk management and supervisory practices, builds compliance content into training schedules and e-learning modules, and the CCO verifies this in the curricula of training institutes; compliance staff are nominated for RBI, IBA and NIBM courses. Inspection and Audit verifies status of compliance with the compliance department's checklist, its findings are a feedback mechanism to the compliance department, and it audits execution of Risk Mitigation Plans and observations in the Risk Assessment Report of RBI. The management audit of the compliance department assesses, among other things, adequacy of staff, sustenance of RBI and external audit observations, quality of regulatory reporting including risk based supervision data, dissemination of instructions and follow up, process improvements and adequacy of the compliance risk assessment framework; compliance risk is included in the risk assessment methodology of internal audit, and the compliance and audit functions are kept separate to avoid conflict of interest.

General guidelines and adverse actions (courseware): staff deal fairly with customers and conduct business consistent with laws and regulations; non-compliance with any regulatory guideline and administrative actions initiated against the bank and corrective steps are disclosed in the bank's Annual Report. Any strictures, show cause notice, cautionary advice or penalty must be reported by the concerned department to the top management and MD and CEO with advice to the compliance department; the head office department prepares a point-wise reply signed by its vertical head and submits it to the compliance department for onward submission, does a root cause analysis, apprises the Board of reasons and corrective action, and reports instantly or monthly to the compliance department.

Divergence disclosure (2025 Directions, Notes to Accounts item (v)): a bank discloses divergence in asset classification and provisioning in a prescribed table if either or both of these conditions hold: (a) the additional provisioning for NPAs assessed by RBI in its supervisory process exceeds 5 per cent of the reported profit before provisions and contingencies for the reference period; (b) the additional gross NPAs identified by RBI exceed 5 per cent of the reported incremental gross NPAs (additions during the reference year) for the reference period. The disclosure is made in the Notes to Accounts of the annual financial statements published immediately after RBI communicates the divergence. The courseware also mentions a SEBI circular of 31 October 2019 requiring disclosure within 24 hours of the final Risk Assessment Report; that is not verified and not taught.
facts.locator: RBI_FS_2025 Notes to Accounts item (v); S01 printed p. 604

facts.statement: Material compliance failure and accountability (courseware): compliance has two levels, Level 1 adherence to external rules (RBI, SEBI, IRDA, IBA, FIMMDA, FEDAI and others) and Level 2 adherence to internal policies, processes, manuals and directions. Non-compliance arises from business verticals, from Inspection and Audit findings and from regulatory inspections by regulators, independent bodies or the Government of India. The compliance department tests compliance at zones, head office and overseas centres; whether a failure is material depends on the detriment or risk of detriment to the bank, the scale of the issue, the overall impact on the bank and its clients, and the extent of loss of confidence in the bank or in the provision of legal services. Accountability categories include non-compliance with laws, regulations, guidelines, policies and approved protocols including Risk Assessment Report and Risk Mitigation Plan (RAR/RMP) requirements, wrongful or inaccurate release of data (accident, negligence or malice), data hoarding and inadequate supervision; responses may be facilitative or punitive and proportionate to the risk and harm. On an allegation, the CCO forms a preliminary inquiry committee of any two of the Assistant General Manager (Risk), AGM (Human Resources) and AGM (Compliance), using the senior-most Chief Manager if an AGM is unavailable; on its report the Inquiry Committee initiates the investigation, which the CCO may have conducted by any officer within a reasonable time such as 15 working days, and the CCO submits findings to the ACB and MD and CEO.

Internal control (courseware): effective internal control gives reasonable assurance that operations are efficient and effective, transactions are recorded accurately, financial reporting is reliable, risk management systems are effective and the bank complies with laws, regulations, policies and procedures; because people execute controls, they remain subject to execution risk. Controls typically limit authorities, safeguard access to and use of records and assets, separate and rotate duties, and ensure regular and unscheduled reviews, including testing. The five components: control environment (organisational structure, management philosophy and operating style, integrity, ethics and competence of personnel, external influences, attention of the Board and its committees, human resources policies); risk assessment; control activities; accounting, information and communication systems; self-assessment or monitoring. Control activities include reviews of operating performance and exception reports, approvals and authorisations (including dual signatures above limits), segregation of duties (and absence of officers in sensitive positions for two consecutive weeks each year), design and use of documents and records (pre-numbered documents), safeguards on access to and use of assets and records, and independent checks such as reconciliation. Six aspects deserve special attention: information systems (integrity, security, privacy and a tested contingency plan), segregation of duties, the audit programme (independent audit function reporting to the Board; annual audit plan; verification of members' accounts at least once every two years), record keeping, protection of physical assets (dual control, access limits) and education of staff (training and cross-training).

Compliance culture and RBI expectations (courseware): banking is moving to a digital model with more service providers, so supervisors stress early warning signals; compliance should go beyond what is legally binding to higher standards of integrity and ethics, with culture shaped by tone from the top, incentive structure, accountability, effective communication, transparency, awareness and controls. Compliance is to protect five customer rights: the Right to Fair Treatment; the Right to Transparency, Fair and Honest Dealing (one right); the Right to Suitability; the Right to Privacy; and the Right to Grievance Redress and Compensation. Inadequate compliance culture raises the risk of legal or regulatory sanctions, business restrictions, material financial loss and reputational damage. RBI expectations in risk based supervision: business functions, risk management, compliance and internal audit are the three lines of defence; the Board puts policies in place documenting the purpose, authority and responsibility of oversight and assurance functions; oversight functions are independent of business with a co-operative relationship, have the same stature as business verticals, sufficient staff and experienced, qualified employees; the Board maintains a quality assurance and improvement programme (with external assessment) covering all aspects; the Board sets up independent and effective assurance functions and exercises oversight, and senior management must not interfere with their independence; compliance is a core activity of the entity and must not be outsourced; the compliance function apprises the Board and senior management and ensures supervisory observations are met in letter and spirit in a time bound and sustainable manner.

payload.title: Adverse actions, divergence disclosure and Annual Report disclosures
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Courseware (needs_review):** non-compliance with regulatory guidelines and **administrative action** taken against the bank, with **corrective steps**, is **disclosed in the Annual Report**. A **strictures, show cause notice, cautionary advice or penalty** is reported to **top management and the MD and CEO** with advice to Compliance; the **head office department** prepares a **point-wise reply signed by its vertical head**, does a **root cause analysis**, tells the **Board** the **reasons and corrective action**, and reports **instantly or monthly** to Compliance.

**Divergence disclosure (2025 Directions, verified).** After a supervisory review, the bank discloses divergence in asset classification and provisioning in the **Notes to Accounts** if **either** holds:

1. RBI's **additional provisioning** is **more than 5% of reported profit before provisions and contingencies**; or
2. RBI's **additional gross NPAs** are **more than 5% of reported incremental gross NPAs**.

The note appears in the **annual statements published right after RBI communicates the divergence**.

payload.title: Does this bank have to disclose a divergence?
payload.core_explanation_md: After a supervisory review, Bank P reports **profit before provisions and contingencies of Rs 2,000 crore** and **incremental gross NPAs of Rs 1,800 crore** for the reference year. RBI assesses **additional provisioning of Rs 130 crore** and **additional gross NPAs of Rs 95 crore**. Bank Q has profit before provisions and contingencies of Rs 2,500 crore, incremental gross NPAs of Rs 2,000 crore, additional provisioning of Rs 100 crore and additional gross NPAs of Rs 80 crore. Decide for each bank whether disclosure is required.

worked_steps.description: Bank P: the provisioning threshold is 5 per cent of profit before provisions and contingencies.
Bank P: RBI's additional provisioning compared with the threshold.
Bank P: the gross NPA threshold is 5 per cent of incremental gross NPAs.
Bank P: additional gross NPAs compared with the threshold.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Condition (b) met, so disclosure is required (either condition is enough)

worked_steps.description: Bank Q: compare each with RBI's figures.
worked_steps.formula_or_substitution: 100 is not more than 125; 80 is not more than 100
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Neither condition met, so no divergence disclosure is required

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Bank P must disclose (both conditions met); Bank Q need not disclose

**Is a failure material?** Weigh the **detriment or risk of detriment** to the bank, the **scale** of the issue, the **overall impact** on the bank and its clients, and the **loss of confidence** in the bank or in providing legal services.

items.title: Responsibility of the Board
items.core_explanation_md:
**RBI rule (circular of 11 September 2020):** the **Board is overall responsible** for overseeing the compliance function and compliance risk. The **MD and CEO** makes sure an **independent compliance function** exists and the **policy is followed**. The policy is **reviewed at least yearly**; its **quality assurance programme** has an **independent external review at least once in three years**; the compliance function is **internally audited**.

**The courseware adds (needs_review):** the Board ensures an **appropriate policy** is in place and implemented, that issues are **resolved expeditiously**, that there is **no conflict of interest** and that **compliance and audit stay separate**; it **reviews compliance quarterly** and the **status annually**, and may **delegate to the ACB**. Under the **Companies Act, 2013**, directors must devise systems to ensure compliance with applicable laws, **confirmed in the Directors' Responsibility Statement**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The three-year external review is a floor; the policy itself is reviewed every year.

self_check.prompt_text: How often must the quality assurance programme of the compliance function be reviewed externally?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At least once in three years.

items.title: The compliance department at the corporate office
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware).

The department has **formal status** at the **central or head office**, headed by the **CCO**, a **senior executive** (preferably a **General Manager or equivalent**, **not below two levels from the CEO**; may be **recruited from the market**).

| Question | Basis |
| --- | --- |
| **What must be complied with?** | **RBI master circulars and directions**, **RBI guidelines**, **laws and statutes** for banks, **internal guidelines and policies** |
| **How risky is it?** | **Regulatory focus**, **nature of activity** (inherently high risk), **exposure and materiality**, **history of breaches** |

**Independence:** compliance staff are **never given audit or inspection duties**; the function is **independently reviewed**; **compliance and audit stay separate**. Staff should be **adequate and well qualified**, preferably with knowledge of **law, accountancy and IT**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Mixing compliance with audit would let one function mark its own work, so they are kept apart.

self_check.prompt_text: Why are compliance staff not assigned audit or inspection duties?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It creates a conflict of interest.

items.title: Adverse actions, divergence disclosure and Annual Report disclosures
items.core_explanation_md:
**Courseware (needs_review):** non-compliance with regulatory guidelines and **administrative action** taken against the bank, with **corrective steps**, is **disclosed in the Annual Report**. A **strictures, show cause notice, cautionary advice or penalty** is reported to **top management and the MD and CEO** with advice to Compliance; the **head office department** prepares a **point-wise reply signed by its vertical head**, does a **root cause analysis**, tells the **Board** the **reasons and corrective action**, and reports **instantly or monthly** to Compliance.

**Divergence disclosure (2025 Directions, verified).** After a supervisory review, the bank discloses divergence in asset classification and provisioning in the **Notes to Accounts** if **either** holds:

1. RBI's **additional provisioning** is **more than 5% of reported profit before provisions and contingencies**; or
2. RBI's **additional gross NPAs** are **more than 5% of reported incremental gross NPAs**.

The note appears in the **annual statements published right after RBI communicates the divergence**.

**Not taught:** the courseware's SEBI 24-hour disclosure requirement, which was not verified.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Either condition alone triggers disclosure; both need not be met.

self_check.prompt_text: Must both divergence conditions be met before disclosure?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; either one is enough.

items.title: Material compliance failures and accountability
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware).

**Two levels of compliance:** **Level 1** is adherence to **external rules** (RBI, SEBI, IRDA, IBA, FIMMDA, FEDAI); **Level 2** is adherence to the bank's **own policies, processes and manuals**. Non-compliance arises from **business verticals**, **Inspection and Audit** findings and **regulatory inspections**.

**Is a failure material?** Weigh the **detriment or risk of detriment** to the bank, the **scale** of the issue, the **overall impact** on the bank and its clients, and the **loss of confidence** in the bank or in providing legal services.

**Accountability:** examples include **breaching laws, rules or policies (including RAR/RMP requirements)**, **wrongful or inaccurate release of data** (accident, negligence or malice), **data hoarding** and **inadequate supervision**. Responses may be **facilitative or punitive** but **proportionate**.

**Inquiry:** the **CCO forms a preliminary inquiry committee of any two of AGM (Risk), AGM (HR) and AGM (Compliance)** (the **senior-most Chief Manager** stands in if an AGM is unavailable); if it finds grounds, the **Inquiry Committee** starts an **investigation** done within a **reasonable time such as 15 working days**; the **CCO reports findings to the ACB and the MD and CEO**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The two-of-three committee spreads the inquiry across risk, HR and compliance so no single function decides alone.

self_check.prompt_text: Who forms the preliminary inquiry committee, and from whom?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The CCO, from any two of the AGMs for Risk, HR and Compliance.

| **Information systems** | **Integrity, security, privacy**; a **tested contingency plan** |

| **Record keeping** | Books follow **sound accounting principles** |
| **Protection of physical assets** | **Dual control**, access limits, physical security |
